rv.q: O'Dell and the director, Karen Carpenter, throw one emotional punch after another; most of them land, but the barrage may leave you reeling.
Under the direction of Karen Carpenter, the actors all give respectable performances.

The play offers few surprises, but the storytelling is interesting and absorbing without any new perceptions. Batt is both suave and acerbic as a man who gives as good as he gets. Canada has authority and gravitas as the African American writer who has become a staple of the American educational syllabus but can’t justify the choices he has made.
Indeed, for a work about writing, publishing, and literary legacies, there is a certain amount of irony that after attending Pay the Writer , I was mostly thinking about the actors.
Sadly, 'Pay the Writer,' is too writerly for its own good.

None of it is enough to make Pay the Writer a story audiences will much care about. For all the personality the actors bring to their characters, this is still a play about a writer and his agent — navel-gazing inside baseball of the worst variety.
Pay the Writer is a rambling, unfocused, undramatic account of the torments of being a successful novelist.
O'Dell is aided by actors who are confident in the characters they're portraying.
Ron Canada's Cyrus is grounded and real. We observe ego, intelligence, stubbornness, rue, affection, and resolution.
On the night in question the show I saw disappointed my high hopes.

My engagement with the work started to unravel as each subplot was brought to a heartfelt moment and the audience was shown where each and every character would be going after the show’s conclusion. It felt less and less meaningful as there was less and less for me to think about.

The tonal shifts in the play can be jarring. Under Karen Carpenter's uneven direction, the cast veers from sitcom lurches for the punchline to feints at naturalism — and the physical production is similarly scattered...
O'Dell's Pay the Writer will likely soon be forgotten — and difficult for budget-strapped regional theaters to produce with an unnecessary cast of eight.
But then by the end, I'm not sure we care enough at all.
Yet it has a kind of low-rent look to it and clunky staging.
